headline: Taste evolved to guide us toward nutrients and away from poisons
universal_truth: Our preferences often have deeper roots than we realize
fun_facts: Humans can detect five basic tastes: sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami
Bitter taste is the most sensitive—we can detect it at much lower concentrations than others
80% of what we call 'taste' is actually smell—that's why food is bland when you have a cold
discussion_questions: Why do you think children often hate bitter vegetables but love sweet foods?
How does knowing taste is mostly smell change how you think about eating?
What food preferences have changed as you've gotten older?

hook.title: Welcome
hook.script: Close your eyes and imagine biting into a lemon. Feel that? Your mouth might actually pucker. Taste is more than sensation—it's survival guidance. Sweet means energy. Bitter warns of poison. Taste evolved to keep you alive.

options.text: I want to learn something new
options.response: Perfect. Curiosity is the first step to understanding. Let's explore this together.
That curiosity is exactly what we need. Let's dive in and discover something amazing.

cliff.title: The Question
cliff.script: We have five taste sensations, but we experience thousands of flavors. How do just five basic inputs create the infinite variety of food experiences? What's happening beyond the tongue?
cliff.prompt: How do we experience so many flavors from just five tastes?

options.text: Smell combines with taste to create most of what we call flavor
options.response: Yes. About 80% of flavor comes from smell. That's why food tastes flat when you're congested.

options.text: Different combinations of the five tastes create all possible flavors
options.response: Combinations matter, but the major player is smell...

q1.title: Survival Sensors
q1.script: Sweet means calories—energy for survival. Salty indicates minerals your body needs. Sour can signal unripe or spoiled food. Bitter warns of potential poison. Umami detects protein. Each taste guides survival decisions.
q1.prompt: What's your first impression of "Survival Sensors"?

options.text: This confirms what I already knew
options.response: Great foundation! Now let's build on that knowledge with something you might not expect...
Perfect starting point! This insight will connect to even more surprising facts ahead.

q2.title: Bitter Defense
q2.script: We're most sensitive to bitter taste—able to detect it at far lower concentrations than other tastes. Why? Many poisons are bitter. Evolution made us extremely good at detecting what might kill us.
q2.prompt: How does this connect to what you already know?

options.response: Exactly. These connections are how knowledge becomes understanding.

options.text: I need to think about this more
options.response: That's a good instinct. Deep understanding takes time. The next fact will help clarify.

q3.title: Smell Is Flavor
q3.script: About 80% of what we call taste is actually smell. Aromas from food travel up the back of your throat to your nose. Hold your nose and eat something—it becomes almost flavorless. Taste and smell are partners.
q3.prompt: What surprises you most about this?

options.text: I never thought about it this way
options.response: That shift in perspective is exactly the point. New angles reveal new truths.
That's learning in action. When understanding shifts, you're really getting it.

wisdom.title: Today's Wisdom
wisdom.script: Here's today's wisdom: Our preferences have deeper roots than we know. Taste reminds us that what we like and dislike often connects to ancient survival needs. Understanding why can help us work with our instincts, not against them.
wisdom.prompt: What resonates most with you today?

options.response: That central truth will stay with you. Let it guide your thinking.
Application is where knowledge becomes wisdom. That's the real learning.

outro.title: See You Tomorrow
outro.script: That's Day 81. Tomorrow, we'll discover why smell triggers memory. Until then, eat something and notice: is it your tongue or your nose doing most of the work?
outro.prompt: Before you go—what will you take from today?

options.response: Reflection deepens learning. Let these ideas simmer in your mind.
Teaching others is the best way to learn. You've already begun the ripple.

growTrack.title: Preference Archaeology - Dig Into Your Tastes
growTrack.learning_objective: Understand the roots of your preferences
growTrack.activity: Pick a food you love or hate. Ask: might this preference connect to something deeper—a survival instinct, a childhood association, a cultural pattern? Understanding our preferences helps us navigate them consciously.
